graph_metadata.title: Git — Full Detail Knowledge Graph
graph_metadata.description: Machine-readable knowledge graph of Git's history, architecture, object model, refs, commands, merge algorithms, transports, server/hosting ecosystem, extensions, workflows, implementations and security lessons.
graph_metadata.source_policy: Based primarily on the user-supplied Git article text. Inferences and operational best-practice rules are labeled as derived rules; claims that can change by version are preserved as source-reported rather than silently updated.

entities.name: Git
entities.description: Distributed version control system for tracking versions of source code and data; each repository ordinarily contains local history and supports independent work and synchronization.

entities.name: Distributed version control
entities.description: Version-control model in which developers hold local repositories and exchange changes between peers.

entities.name: Version control system
entities.description: System that records changes to files over time and supports history inspection and collaboration.

entities.name: Source code management
entities.description: Management of source-code versions and collaborative development history.

entities.name: Linus Torvalds
entities.description: Created Git in 2005 to support Linux kernel development after the loss of the BitKeeper arrangement.

entities.name: Junio C. Hamano
entities.description: Major contributor who took over maintenance in July 2005 and led the Git 1.0 release.

entities.name: Linux kernel
entities.description: Large distributed open-source kernel project whose development needs motivated Git.

entities.name: BitKeeper
entities.description: Proprietary source-control system used for Linux kernel development from 2002 until its free-license arrangement was revoked.

entities.name: Mercurial
entities.description: Distributed version-control system whose creation was also spurred by the BitKeeper incident.

entities.name: Concurrent Versions System (CVS)
entities.description: Earlier version-control system used by Torvalds as a design example of what Git should avoid.

entities.name: Git official website
entities.description: Official Git project website.

entities.name: Git source repository
entities.description: Canonical Git source-code repository hosted at git.kernel.org.

entities.name: GNU General Public License version 2.0 only
entities.description: Git is identified as GPL-2.0-only, with some components under compatible licenses such as LGPLv2.1.

entities.name: C
entities.description: Primary implementation language for Git.

entities.name: Shell script
entities.description: Used for wrappers and scripts in Git's toolkit-based design.

entities.name: Perl
entities.description: Used in Git tooling and in the Windows distribution environment.

entities.name: Python
entities.description: Used for tooling and in independent Git implementations.

entities.name: Tcl
entities.description: Used for the Tcl/Tk GUI distributed with Git.

entities.name: Windows
entities.description: Supported operating system; historical case-insensitive filesystem behavior was relevant to a Git vulnerability.

entities.name: macOS
entities.description: Supported operating system; historical case-insensitive filesystem behavior was relevant to a Git vulnerability.

entities.name: Linux
entities.description: Primary development environment for Git.

entities.name: POSIX systems
entities.description: Includes Linux, macOS, Solaris, AIX and related environments cited for Git support.

entities.name: Distributed workflow
entities.description: Development model where repository histories and changes move between independently held repositories.

entities.name: Central integration repository
entities.description: Commonly used shared remote repository that hosts an integrated copy despite Git's peer-to-peer repository model.

entities.name: Local repository
entities.description: Repository stored on a developer's computer with local history and version-tracking data.

entities.name: Remote repository
entities.description: Another repository, commonly on a server, from or to which changes are fetched or pushed.

entities.name: Offline repository operation
entities.description: Local history and operations remain available without network access.

entities.name: Performance and scalability
entities.description: Git design goals include fast patching, efficient history access and support for large projects.

entities.name: Data integrity
entities.description: Safeguards against accidental or malicious corruption were explicit design goals.

entities.name: Non-linear development history
entities.description: History with multiple branches and concurrent lines of development.

entities.name: Branch
entities.description: Lightweight named reference to a commit; branch names can advance as commits are added.

entities.name: Commit object
entities.description: Immutable object connecting a tree snapshot to parent commits and metadata including author/committer information, timestamps and a log message.

entities.name: Tree object
entities.description: Directory-like snapshot listing names, mode/type bits and references to blobs or other trees.

entities.name: Blob object
entities.description: Object containing file contents without filename or timestamps; its identity is content-derived.

entities.name: Annotated tag object
entities.description: Object referring to another object and carrying metadata, often including a digital signature for a release.

entities.name: Packfile
entities.description: Compressed bundle of Git objects, often using delta compression for storage and transport efficiency.

entities.name: Git object database
entities.description: Stores immutable Git objects such as blobs, trees, commits, tags and packed objects.

entities.name: Git index / staging area
entities.description: Mutable cache between working tree and object database; records what is staged for the next commit.

entities.name: Working tree
entities.description: Checked-out files and directories on which a user works.

entities.name: Git references (refs)
entities.description: Named pointers that identify commits or other objects; include branches, tags, remotes and other namespaces.

entities.name: HEAD
entities.description: Reserved reference identifying the current checkout context, commonly the current branch or commit.

entities.name: Local branch refs
entities.description: Named local branch references that normally advance when new commits are made on them.

entities.name: Git tags
entities.description: References used to label important points in history; lightweight tags point directly to an object, annotated tags use tag objects.

entities.name: Remote-tracking references
entities.description: Local references representing observed state of branches in remote repositories.

entities.name: Git stash
entities.description: Mechanism for saving uncommitted work for later reapplication; the source describes stash refs as objects not yet committed.

entities.name: .gitignore
entities.description: Plain-text patterns describing files Git should not track, commonly used for generated files, secrets and large files.

entities.name: Content hash
entities.description: Digest computed from object content and used as an object identifier.

entities.name: SHA-1
entities.description: Historically used by Git for object IDs and pack integrity checks; the source describes Git's response to the SHAttered collision demonstration.

entities.name: SHAttered attack
entities.description: 2017 demonstration of practical SHA-1 collision capability that prompted Git hardening and hash-transition planning.

entities.name: Git hash-function transition
entities.description: Git work to transition away from dependence on SHA-1, with planning noted as ongoing since February 2020 in the source.

entities.name: Merkle tree
entities.description: Hash-linked tree where a root hash identifies the content and structure beneath it; Git's tree/commit structure has this property.

entities.name: zlib compression
entities.description: Compression used for Git objects and packfiles.

entities.name: Delta compression
entities.description: Stores object differences relative to similar objects to reduce packfile size.

entities.name: git gc
entities.description: Garbage collection and maintenance command that can prune eligible unreachable objects and repack objects.

entities.name: git fsck
entities.description: Checks repository object integrity and connectivity.

entities.name: git init
entities.description: Creates a new local repository; the default initial branch name is configurable and varies by Git version/configuration.

entities.name: git clone
entities.description: Creates a copy of a repository from a local path or remote URL.

entities.name: git add
entities.description: Adds selected working-tree content to the index/staging area.

entities.name: git commit
entities.description: Records the staged state as a new commit in repository history.

entities.name: git fetch
entities.description: Retrieves objects and refs from a remote without necessarily integrating them into the current branch.

entities.name: git pull
entities.description: Fetches from a remote and integrates changes, usually by merge or rebase according to configuration.

entities.name: git push
entities.description: Publishes local refs and reachable commits to a remote repository subject to permissions and server policy.

entities.name: git merge
entities.description: Integrates changes from one or more histories into the current branch.

entities.name: git rebase
entities.description: Replays commits onto another base, rewriting commit identities for the replayed history.

entities.name: git revert
entities.description: Creates a new commit that reverses an earlier commit without removing the original published commit from history.

entities.name: git show-ref
entities.description: Lists references known to the repository.

entities.name: git daemon
entities.description: Built-in simple TCP server for Git protocol; the source notes typical port 9418.

entities.name: gitweb
entities.description: CGI-based web interface for browsing Git repository contents over HTTP.

entities.name: Git GUI
entities.description: Tcl/Tk graphical interface distributed with Git.

entities.name: Git LFS
entities.description: Extension that supports handling large files outside ordinary Git object storage.

entities.name: git-annex
entities.description: Distributed file synchronization system based on Git.

entities.name: git-flow
entities.description: Extensions and conventions for feature/develop/main/hotfix branching.

entities.name: git-machete
entities.description: Repository organizer and automation for rebase, merge, pull and push operations.

entities.name: Virtual File System for Git
entities.description: Extension using placeholders for files in very large repositories and downloading file contents when accessed.

entities.name: Pull request / merge request
entities.description: A hosting-service workflow requesting that a branch be merged into another; not a core Git SCM feature.

entities.name: Code review
entities.description: Review of proposed changes, often supported by pull/merge requests and hosting services.

entities.name: Merge conflict
entities.description: Condition where Git cannot automatically reconcile changes and requires manual resolution.

entities.name: Three-way merge
entities.description: Merge algorithm using two branch tips and a common ancestor as inputs.

entities.name: resolve merge strategy
entities.description: Traditional three-way merge strategy.

entities.name: recursive merge strategy
entities.description: Historical strategy described by the source as a variant of three-way merge, able to combine multiple merge bases and handle renames; current Git versions may use newer strategy names.

entities.name: octopus merge strategy
entities.description: Strategy used by default when merging more than two heads, according to the source.

entities.name: Rename detection
entities.description: Git infers renames when browsing snapshot history by similarity rather than recording persistent file identity at commit time.

entities.name: File history traversal
entities.description: History inspection may walk project-wide commits and determine which changed a particular file.

entities.name: Git server
entities.description: A repository made accessible over a network or remote shell; Git can serve repositories using built-in or dedicated services.

entities.name: Git protocol
entities.description: Protocol used to exchange Git objects and refs; the built-in daemon listens on TCP port 9418.

entities.name: HTTP
entities.description: One transport for publishing and accessing repositories.

entities.name: HTTPS
entities.description: Encrypted HTTP transport for repository access.

entities.name: SSH
entities.description: Remote-shell and Git transport option for authenticated repository access.

entities.name: FTP
entities.description: Transport listed in the source as historically supported for repository publication.

entities.name: CVS server emulation
entities.description: Allows existing CVS clients and IDE plugins to access Git through a CVS-compatible interface.

entities.name: git-svn
entities.description: Tool that allows Subversion repositories to be used through Git workflows.

entities.name: Git protocol v2
entities.description: Client-directed protocol version designed to avoid advertising every ref before the client indicates what it wants.

entities.name: Gerrit
entities.description: Git server and code-review tool with configurable authentication/integration options and pull-request functionality.

entities.name: Phabricator
entities.description: Code collaboration suite with Git support, noted as less prominent in Facebook's Mercurial-centered environment.

entities.name: RhodeCode Community Edition
entities.description: Self-hosting source-control solution supporting Git, Mercurial and Subversion.

entities.name: Kallithea
entities.description: Python-based self-hosting service supporting Git and Mercurial.

entities.name: gitolite
entities.description: Scripts and tooling that add fine-grained access control for Git repositories.

entities.name: Gogs
entities.description: Self-hosted Git service implemented in Go.

entities.name: Gitea
entities.description: Self-hosted Git service forked from Gogs and implemented in Go.

entities.name: Forgejo
entities.description: Self-hosted Git service forked from Gitea and implemented in Go.

entities.name: GitHub
entities.description: Git repository hosting and collaboration service; pull requests are a hosting-layer feature.

entities.name: GitLab
entities.description: Git repository hosting and collaboration service, including merge requests.

entities.name: Bitbucket
entities.description: Git repository hosting service.

entities.name: SourceForge
entities.description: Software project hosting service offering Git repositories.

entities.name: JGit
entities.description: Pure Java implementation/library of Git embedded in Java applications; used by Gerrit and EGit.

entities.name: go-git
entities.description: Pure Go implementation of Git.

entities.name: Dulwich
entities.description: Pure Python implementation of Git.

entities.name: libgit2
entities.description: ANSI C Git library with language bindings.

entities.name: JS-Git
entities.description: JavaScript implementation of a subset of Git.

entities.name: Game of Trees
entities.description: Independent Git-compatible implementation associated with OpenBSD.

entities.name: git9
entities.description: Independent Git implementation for Plan 9.

entities.name: gitoxide
entities.description: Git implementation written in Rust.

entities.name: EGit
entities.description: Git client integration for the Eclipse IDE using JGit.

entities.name: GTK
entities.description: Toolkit used by gitg graphical front-end.

entities.name: gitg
entities.description: Graphical Git front-end using GTK.

entities.name: Open-source software
entities.description: Software whose source is available under an open-source license.

entities.name: Version history
entities.description: Ordered/branched record of repository snapshots and their relationships.

entities.name: Snapshot-based versioning
entities.description: Git records snapshots of directory trees rather than explicit persistent file identities or per-file revision chains.

entities.name: Working copy
entities.description: Checked-out version of repository files in a working tree.

entities.name: origin remote
entities.description: Common default name for the remote from which a repository was cloned.

entities.name: main branch
entities.description: Common default integration branch name used by several hosting services; source reports Git's planned change to main for a future 3.0 release.

entities.name: master branch
entities.description: Historical default initial branch name; not intrinsically special in Git.

entities.name: feature/* branch
entities.description: Branch naming convention for feature-specific unstable development.

entities.name: develop branch
entities.description: Integration branch convention for ongoing development in git-flow.

entities.name: hotfix branch
entities.description: Branch convention for emergency patches to released products.

entities.name: Reflog
entities.description: Local record of reference movements that can help recover recently reachable commits; not explicitly detailed in the source article.

entities.name: Git hooks
entities.description: Executable scripts that Git can run at certain repository events; unsafe hook content was central to a historical vulnerability.

entities.name: Git configuration
entities.description: Repository or user configuration including aliases and remote settings.

entities.name: .gitmodules
entities.description: File that can define submodule URLs; attacker-controlled URLs were involved in a historical vulnerability.

entities.name: CVE-2014-9390 / malicious .git directory issue
entities.description: Historical Windows/macOS vulnerability involving case-insensitive filesystems, malicious .git-like directories, hooks and configuration.

entities.name: CVE-2015-7545
entities.description: Historical vulnerability fixed in Git 2.6.1 involving crafted clone URLs and possible arbitrary command execution.

entities.name: Man-in-the-middle attack
entities.description: Network attacker intercepts or alters communications; the source notes an unencrypted connection could enable redirection to a malicious clone URL.

entities.name: Repository access control
entities.description: Authorization mechanisms commonly supplied by surrounding server or hosting tools rather than Git's core object model.

entities.name: Digital signature
entities.description: Cryptographic signature used to authenticate tags/commits or releases; source emphasizes signing as an important security layer.

entities.name: Signed Git tag
entities.description: Annotated tag can carry a digital signature for a release object.

entities.name: Secret management hygiene
entities.description: Prevent credentials, keys and passwords from entering repository history; .gitignore can prevent accidental tracking but is not a substitute for secret scanning or history cleanup.

entities.name: Large files
entities.description: Files that may be better managed with Git LFS or other dedicated storage.

entities.name: Repository fork
entities.description: Independent repository copy used to develop changes and submit them for integration.

entities.name: Push and history policy
entities.description: Published commits are normally preserved; reverting is safer for shared history, while sensitive-data removal may require rewriting history and coordinating cleanup.

entities.name: Source article: Git (Wikipedia text supplied by user)
entities.description: User-supplied article text describing Git; claims and version-specific details in this graph are based on that source.

entities.name: Immutable object model
entities.description: Git objects are content-addressed and treated as immutable once written.

entities.name: Unreachable objects
entities.description: Objects not reachable from references or other objects may eventually be pruned by garbage collection.

entities.name: Loose objects
entities.description: Newly created objects stored individually in the object database before packing.

entities.name: Pack index
entities.description: Index mapping packed object identifiers to offsets in a packfile.

entities.name: Commit metadata
entities.description: Commit records tree, parent commit references, timestamp and log message; Git commit objects also encode author/committer identity and timestamps.

entities.name: Repository integrity checking
entities.description: Validation of object integrity/connectivity with git fsck and checksum verification.

entities.name: Patch
entities.description: A set of changes applied to source files; fast patch application was a design target.

entities.name: Linux kernel 2.6.12 release
entities.description: Git managed this kernel release on 16 June 2005.

entities.name: Self-hosting
entities.description: A project uses its own system to manage its development; Git became self-hosting on 7 April 2005.

entities.name: First multi-branch merge in Git
entities.description: First merge of multiple branches took place on 18 April 2005.

entities.name: Git 1.0 release
entities.description: Release managed by Junio Hamano on 21 December 2005.

entities.name: Git 2.2.1
entities.description: Release on 17 December 2014 that fixed the malicious .git directory vulnerability described in the source.

entities.name: Git 2.6.1
entities.description: Release on 29 September 2015 that patched CVE-2015-7545.

entities.name: Git 2.56.0
entities.description: Stable release reported by the supplied article as released 28 September 2026.

entities.name: TCP port 9418
entities.description: Typical port for the built-in Git daemon protocol.

entities.name: Repository metadata
entities.description: Information associated with repository objects, refs, configuration and commit messages.

entities.name: Public-key cryptography
entities.description: External concept referenced for signed tags and release authentication; expected to be connected to a separate public-key cryptography graph.

architecture_patterns.name: Local edit-to-commit lifecycle
architecture_patterns.description: Stages a selected working-tree state and records it as a new snapshot in local history.

steps.action: Edit files in the working tree
effects: working_tree changes
index updated
new commit and tree objects
current branch ref advances
review local history and remaining changes

architecture_patterns.name: Distributed collaboration lifecycle
architecture_patterns.description: Copies repository history locally, develops a branch, and publishes it to a remote repository.

effects: local repository and working tree created
branch ref points to current commit
local commits extend branch history
remote-tracking refs and objects updated
remote receives commits/ref if policy permits

steps.action: Request review through hosting service if used
effects: pull/merge request opened outside core Git

architecture_patterns.name: Merge and conflict-resolution workflow
architecture_patterns.description: Integrates divergent branch histories using a merge strategy and asks for manual resolution when necessary.

effects: remote state becomes available locally
Git calculates merge result from history/common ancestor
manual edits reconcile competing changes
index records resolutions
merge commit records multiple parents where applicable

architecture_patterns.name: Object storage and packing lifecycle
architecture_patterns.description: Represents files and snapshots as immutable content-addressed objects, then compacts objects into packfiles.

effects: blob IDs derive from content hashes
tree entries link names/modes to blobs and subtrees
commit references root tree and parent commits
fast object creation, more filesystem entries
packfiles and indexes improve storage/transfer efficiency
integrity/connectivity checks run

architecture_patterns.name: Release authentication pattern
architecture_patterns.description: Use an annotated signed tag to identify and authenticate a release point.

effects: release state exists in history
tag object contains metadata and signature
remote receives tag subject to policy

steps.action: Verify signer and tag before consuming release
effects: signature verification supports publisher authentication

architecture_patterns.name: Prevent and remediate secret exposure
architecture_patterns.description: Reduce the chance that credentials are committed and define remediation if a secret enters history.

steps.action: Ignore local secret/config files where appropriate
effects: untracked matching files are excluded

steps.action: Use secret scanning and pre-commit checks
effects: credentials can be detected before publication

steps.action: If a secret was committed, revoke or rotate it immediately
effects: exposed credential is no longer trusted

steps.action: Coordinate history cleanup and remote cleanup
effects: sensitive content may be removed by history rewrite, but clones/caches may retain copies

steps.action: Use revert rather than rewriting ordinary shared history
effects: published shared history remains stable for routine changes

architecture_patterns.name: Secure repository transport and authorization
architecture_patterns.description: Separate transport security from repository authorization and signed-history verification.

effects: protects transport and/or authenticates remote depending on configuration

steps.action: Enforce repository permissions at server/hosting layer
effects: read/write access constrained by policy

steps.action: Review untrusted clone URLs, submodule URLs and hooks
effects: reduces malicious repository/config execution risk

steps.action: Verify signed release tags or commits when provided
effects: authenticates signer for signed content; hashes alone do not prove identity
receives security fixes for known vulnerabilities

architecture_patterns.name: Fork-and-review workflow
architecture_patterns.description: Uses an independent repository and hosting-service pull request for collaboration.

steps.action: Fork or clone the upstream repository
effects: independent development copy created

steps.action: Develop commits on a topic branch
effects: change history isolated from upstream default branch

steps.action: Push branch to a writable remote
effects: branch becomes available for review

steps.action: Open pull/merge request on hosting service
effects: review metadata and discussion tracked by forge

steps.action: Review, test and merge through configured process
effects: approved commits integrated into target branch

architecture_patterns.name: Large repository optimization
architecture_patterns.description: Use packing, selective transfer and virtualization/extensions when repository size becomes expensive.

effects: reduced loose-object overhead and delta-compressed storage
fetch can request only relevant refs

steps.action: Use Git LFS for appropriate large binary assets
effects: large payloads handled through LFS workflows

steps.action: Consider VFS for Git for huge working trees
effects: placeholder files downloaded when accessed

steps.action: Measure repository history and clone costs
effects: choose optimization based on workload

derived_rules.title: Local commits are repository-local until published
derived_rules.statement: A successful local commit does not automatically update a remote repository; use push or an explicit hosting workflow to publish changes.

derived_rules.title: Review the index before committing
derived_rules.statement: git commit records staged content, so inspect staged diffs and status to avoid committing unintended changes.

derived_rules.title: A content hash is not publisher authentication
derived_rules.statement: Object hashes support content identity and integrity checks, but signed tags/commits or a trusted release process are needed to authenticate who published content.

derived_rules.title: Do not assume SHA-1 collision resistance
derived_rules.statement: The source documents the SHAttered demonstration and Git's hash-transition work; deployments should follow current Git guidance on hash compatibility and security.

derived_rules.title: Do not treat .gitignore as secret removal
derived_rules.statement: Ignoring a file prevents matching untracked files from being added by ordinary workflows; it does not erase already committed secrets from history or other clones.

derived_rules.title: Rotate exposed credentials before history cleanup
derived_rules.statement: If a credential was committed, revoke/rotate it first; history rewriting alone cannot ensure every clone or cache has discarded the value.

derived_rules.title: Prefer revert for changes already shared
derived_rules.statement: A new revert commit is generally safer for shared published history than rewriting commits on which others may depend.

derived_rules.title: Enforce permissions outside core Git
derived_rules.statement: Git's core does not provide access control; enforce read/write authorization at the server, SSH, hosting or authorization-tool layer.

derived_rules.title: Treat untrusted repositories as executable-risk inputs
derived_rules.statement: Inspect repository configuration, hooks, submodule URLs and scripts before running commands or tools from untrusted repositories.

derived_rules.title: Use authenticated protected transports for remotes
derived_rules.statement: Prefer appropriately configured SSH or HTTPS and verify host identity; an unencrypted or untrusted transport can expose users to redirection or interception.

derived_rules.title: Keep Git clients and servers patched
derived_rules.statement: Historical vulnerabilities were fixed in later releases; update supported clients, servers and hosting services to receive security fixes.

derived_rules.title: Do not rely on unreachable objects as durable backups
derived_rules.statement: Unreachable objects may be removed by automatic or explicit garbage collection; preserve important commits with refs or backups.

derived_rules.title: Rename history is inferred, not stored as permanent file identity
derived_rules.statement: Git detects renames heuristically while viewing history; a rename with substantial simultaneous edits may appear as deletion plus addition.

derived_rules.title: Pull requests belong to hosting/workflow layers
derived_rules.statement: A pull request is not a native Git object or command; Git transports commits and refs while hosting services manage review records and merge UI.

derived_rules.title: Validate merges that require manual conflict resolution
derived_rules.statement: A successful merge operation can still require human judgment; test the integrated result and review staged resolutions before finalizing.

derived_rules.title: Limit unnecessary ref advertisement in large repositories
derived_rules.statement: Where supported, protocol v2 allows clients to request relevant refs, reducing overhead for fetches that need only a subset of repository state.

derived_rules.title: Verify signatures for security-sensitive releases
derived_rules.statement: When a release uses signed tags, verify the signature and trust in the signing key before relying on the tag as publisher-authenticated.

derived_rules.title: Distinguish working tree, index and object database
derived_rules.statement: Working-tree edits are not staged; staged content is not committed; committed objects are local history until pushed.

derived_rules.title: Do not assume every repository uses the same default branch name
derived_rules.statement: Repositories may use main, master or a configured alternative; inspect local and remote refs rather than hard-coding a branch name.

examples.title: Create and commit a local change
examples.scenario: A developer changes a file and wants a recorded snapshot.
examples.outcome: The index contents become a new commit in local history; nothing is published remotely unless pushed.

examples.title: Collaborate on a feature branch
examples.scenario: A developer contributes a feature to a shared repository.
steps: open a pull/merge request on the hosting service
examples.outcome: Commits remain locally available offline, then are published to a remote branch and optionally reviewed using a hosting-layer pull request.

examples.title: Resolve conflicting edits
examples.scenario: Two branches modify overlapping lines and Git cannot automatically choose a result.
steps: edit files to desired combined result
examples.outcome: The resulting history records the integrated state; tests and review are needed to validate semantic correctness.

examples.title: Authenticate a release tag
examples.scenario: A maintainer wants consumers to verify that a release tag was signed by an expected key.
examples.outcome: Signature verification checks the tag signature; consumers must also trust the signer/key and verify release provenance.

examples.title: Respond to a committed credential
examples.scenario: A password or API token accidentally enters a commit and may have been pushed.
steps: Revoke or rotate the credential immediately
Check access logs and downstream use
Coordinate removal/rewriting of affected history if required
Notify collaborators and clean relevant clones/caches where feasible
Add preventive scanning and appropriate ignore rules
examples.outcome: The credential is invalidated first; history cleanup reduces future exposure but cannot guarantee every copy is erased.

examples.title: Inspect repository integrity and storage
examples.scenario: A maintainer wants to check object connectivity and reduce loose-object overhead.
examples.outcome: Integrity checks and object packing can reveal repository issues and improve storage efficiency; garbage collection can prune unreachable objects.

notes: Git is distributed even when a team chooses a central integration server.
Git's content-addressed object store, commit-parent links and tree structure form the basis of its history and integrity model.
Hashes do not by themselves establish the identity or trustworthiness of a publisher; signatures and trusted key distribution address that separate problem.
Hosting features such as pull requests and fine-grained authorization are distinct from core Git objects and commands.

Some source details are explicitly historical (e.g., recursive merge strategy, SHA-1 internals, old vulnerabilities, and planned Git 3.0 default branch change); verify current official documentation before relying on them operationally.
